tip: Ενοικιάζεται (enikiázete) = for rent – the sign you'll see hanging on balconies.
Πήρα (píra) = I took, but with a person it means I phoned: πήρα τον μεσίτη (píra ton mesíti) = I called the agent.
The long unfinished search takes the ongoing past form: ψάχναμε (psákhname) = we kept looking.
Το ρετιρέ (to retiré) = the top-floor flat – a French loan that keeps the same form in every case.
Θέλει (théli) literally means it wants: θέλει δουλειά (théli dhuliá) = it wants work, i.e. it needs work. Greek things want repairs, painting, cleaning.
Greek has no 'to do' form of the verb; a second verb links with να (na): μπορούμε να δούμε (borúme na dhúme) = we can see.
Μάς άρεσε (mas árese) = we liked it – in Greek the house does the pleasing, so το σπίτι (to spíti) is the subject.
Έχει (ékhi) at the start of a sentence = there is: έχει φούρνο απέναντι (ékhi fúrno apénandi) = there's a bakery across the way.
Greek normally uses no word for a when you just have something: έχουμε γάτα (ékhume gháta) = we have cat. Adding μία (mía) would stress exactly one.
Η εγγύηση (i engíisi) = the deposit, and it's counted in rents: δύο ενοίκια (dhío eníkia) = two months' worth.
Το νοίκι (to níki) = the everyday word for ενοίκιο (eníkio), the rent – same meaning, fewer syllables.
Η ΔΕΗ (i dhéi) = the main Greek power company – people often use the name for the electricity bill itself.
Μη (mi) before the ongoing verb form makes an open-ended don't: μη δίνεις (mi dhínis) = don't be giving, as a rule.
Greek normally compares with from, not than: πιο φτηνό από το κέντρο (pio ftinó apó to kéndro) = cheaper than the centre.
Ακριβαίνουν (akrivénun) = they get more expensive – Greek packs the whole phrase into one verb, ακριβαίνω (akrivéno).
Ο/η συγκάτοικος (singátikos) = flatmate – one form covers men and women, so μια συγκάτοικο (mia singátiko) is a female one.
Οι ξένοι (i xéni) here = the guests, not foreigners: έχουμε ξένους (ékhume xénus) = we have company.
Rooms and desks see their view in Greek: βλέπει στο μπαλκόνι (vlépi sto balkóni) = it looks onto the balcony.
Φτιάχνω (ftiákhno) = I make, and also I fix: θα φτιάξει τη βρύση (tha ftiáksi ti vrísi) = he'll fix the tap.
Έπεσε το ρεύμα (épese to révma) = the power fell – that's the everyday way to say the electricity went out.
Οι ασφάλειες (i asfálies) = the fuses, and the same word means insurance – context tells you which.
For something still going on, Greek uses the plain present: κάνουμε κρύο ντους δύο μέρες τώρα (kánume krío dus dhío méres tóra) = we've been taking cold showers for two days.
Greek closes electricity off: κλείσε τον γενικό διακόπτη (klíse ton yenikó dhiakópti) = turn off the main switch; ανοίγω (anígho) = open is how you turn it on.
Στρώνω (stróno) means 'lay flat, smooth out', so έστρωσε (éstrose) = it smoothed into working order. Works for hinges, machines, even the weather.
Κουβαλήσαμε (kuvalísame) = we lugged, from κουβαλάω (kuvaláo) – heavier and sweatier work than plain φέρνω (férno) = bring.
Σαν στο σπίτι μας (san sto spíti mas) = like at our own home; swap the ending for κάνε σαν στο σπίτι σου (káne san sto spíti su) = make yourself at home.
Τι καιρό κάνει; (ti keró káni) = what's the weather like – ο καιρός (o kerós) normally pairs with the verb κάνω (káno), not is.
Θα βρέξει (tha vréksi) = it'll rain, one spell of it; θα βρέχει (tha vrékhi) stresses that it keeps raining.
Greek weather has its temperature: έχει σαράντα βαθμούς (ékhi saránda vathmús) = it has forty degrees, where English says it is forty.
Δεν έκλεισα μάτι (den éklisa máti) is literally 'I didn't close an eye' – Greek counts a single eye where English counts a wink.
